course.title: The Islamic World: History & Civilization
course.description: A journey through fourteen centuries of Islamic history and civilization, from pre-Islamic Arabia and the life of the Prophet Muhammad to the great caliphates, the scientific flowering of the Golden Age, and the modern Islamic world. The course treats the religion and its followers with accuracy and respect, surveying faith, politics, science, art, and empire across three continents. Structure and facts are adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: In the century before Islam, the city of Mecca was important mainly as…
options: a trading center that also held the Kaaba shrine
the capital of the Byzantine Empire
questions.explanation: Mecca sat on caravan routes and held the Kaaba, drawing both merchants and pilgrims — see 'Arabia before Islam'.

questions.prompt: The Prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca around which year?
questions.explanation: Tradition places his birth around 570 CE — see 'The Prophet Muhammad and the birth of Islam'.

questions.prompt: The migration of the early Muslim community from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE is called the…
questions.explanation: The Hijra, in 622 CE, marks year one of the Islamic calendar.

questions.prompt: How many Pillars of Islam are there?
questions.explanation: The Five Pillars are Shahada, Salat, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj.

questions.prompt: The Abbasid caliphate established its capital at…
questions.explanation: The Abbasids founded Baghdad in 762 CE, while the earlier Umayyads had ruled from Damascus.

questions.prompt: The scholar al-Khwarizmi is best known for his foundational work in…
questions.explanation: His treatise on al-jabr founded algebra; the word algorithm also comes from his name.

questions.prompt: Islamic Spain was known in Arabic as…
questions.explanation: Al-Andalus named the Muslim-ruled parts of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 CE.

questions.prompt: The Ottoman conquest of Constantinople took place in…
questions.explanation: Sultan Mehmed II captured the city in 1453 CE, ending the Byzantine Empire.

lessons.title: Arabia before Islam
lessons.grammar_note: Dates in this course use CE (Common Era), which matches the Gregorian years written as AD; the Islamic (Hijri) calendar begins separately in 622 CE.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Picture the Arabian Peninsula around the year 600 CE and explain its geography, its peoples, and its religious life. By the end you will be able to describe the difference between settled town dwellers and nomadic Bedouin tribes, say why the city of Mecca was both a commercial and a religious hub, and name the larger empires that pressed on Arabia from the north. You will also understand the term often used for this era, the Jahiliyyah, and why it should be read with care rather than as a simple insult. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, recall what cube-shaped shrine in Mecca drew pilgrims from across the peninsula, and ask yourself what would make a desert trading town worth fighting over. Keep in mind that the peoples of pre-Islamic Arabia had rich traditions of poetry, trade, and law long before the seventh century, and that this chapter sets the human stage onto which Islam would later emerge.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Arabia in the early 600s CE was a vast peninsula of desert, oasis, and coastline, home to two broad ways of life. Nomadic Bedouin tribes herded camels and sheep and moved with the seasons, bound together by kinship, honor, and a shared code of hospitality and vengeance. Settled communities clustered in oasis towns and along trade routes, where caravans carried incense, spices, and goods between the Indian Ocean, East Africa, and the Mediterranean. Mecca, in the western region of the Hejaz, grew wealthy as a caravan stop and as a pilgrimage center built around the Kaaba, a cube-shaped sanctuary that housed many tribal idols. The dominant religion was polytheism, with each tribe honoring its own gods and spirits, though communities of Jews and Christians also lived in the peninsula, and some individuals, called hanifs, leaned toward a single creator. To the north loomed two superpowers, the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire and the Sasanian Persian Empire, whose long wars exhausted both and left openings along their frontiers. Arabic poetry flourished as the proudest art form, preserving tribal memory and law. This society, often labeled the Jahiliyyah, or age of ignorance, was neither empty nor simple; it was the complex world into which the Prophet Muhammad would be born.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Several landmarks help anchor this period. The Kaaba at Mecca was the peninsula's most important shrine; guardianship of it brought the ruling tribe, the Quraysh, both prestige and income from pilgrims. Trade fairs such as the one at Ukaz doubled as poetry contests, where the finest verses were celebrated across tribes. The Quraysh organized the great trading caravans that traveled north toward Syria in summer and south toward Yemen in winter. Among the powers nearby, the Byzantine Empire held the Levant and Egypt, while the Sasanian Empire ruled Persia and Iraq; their rivalry shaped Arabian politics and commerce. The year 570 CE is traditionally remembered as the Year of the Elephant, when an army is said to have marched against Mecca and failed, and it is the year often given for the birth of the Prophet Muhammad. The clan of Hashim, part of the Quraysh, would be his family. Tribal society had no central state; authority rested with clan elders and with alliances sealed by custom. Understanding these places and figures, the Kaaba, the Quraysh, the caravans, and the two great empires, makes the swift rise of Islam in the following decades far easier to follow.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the two broad ways of life in pre-Islamic Arabia. 2) Which tribe controlled Mecca and guarded the Kaaba? 3) What two great empires bordered Arabia to the north? 4) What was the most prestigious art form of the age? 5) What does the term Jahiliyyah mean, and why should it be used carefully? 6) Why was Mecca both a commercial and a religious center? Answers: 1) Settled town dwellers and nomadic Bedouin tribes. 2) The Quraysh. 3) The Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire and the Sasanian Persian Empire. 4) Arabic poetry, recited and preserved orally and honored at fairs such as Ukaz. 5) It is usually translated as the age of ignorance; it describes the period before Islam from a later religious viewpoint, so it is best understood as a term of contrast rather than a claim that the people were uncultured. 6) It sat on major caravan routes and held the Kaaba, drawing both merchants and pilgrims, which combined wealth with religious prestige for its ruling tribe.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: imagining pre-Islamic Arabia as an empty desert with no culture; in fact it had thriving trade, sophisticated poetry, and established religious practices. Mistake: assuming everyone in Arabia was polytheist; Jewish and Christian communities lived there, and some sought a single creator before Islam arrived. Mistake: treating the Jahiliyyah as a factual label for ignorance rather than a later religious term of contrast. Exit ticket: (a) What was the Kaaba, and in which city did it stand? (b) Which two empires pressed on Arabia from the north, and why did their rivalry matter? Answers: (a) The Kaaba was a cube-shaped shrine in Mecca that housed tribal idols and drew pilgrims from across the peninsula. (b) The Byzantine and Sasanian empires; their long wars drained both and loosened their grip on the frontier regions near Arabia, leaving an opening that later events would fill. Carry these points forward, because the next lesson turns to the man born into this world around 570 CE and the message he would bring.

lessons.title: The Prophet Muhammad and the birth of Islam
lessons.grammar_note: Throughout, the founder of Islam is referred to respectfully as the Prophet Muhammad, and all years are given in CE.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace the life of the Prophet Muhammad from his birth in Mecca around 570 CE to his death in 632 CE, and explain how the community of Islam began. By the end you will be able to outline his early life and reputation, describe the first revelations and his call to worship one God, explain why he and his followers faced opposition in Mecca, and define the Hijra, the migration to Medina that opens the Islamic calendar. You will also be able to say, in plain terms, what Muslims believe about his role as a prophet. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, recall the year of the Hijra and the two cities it connects. As you read, treat this as a careful historical and respectful account; Muslims regard the Prophet Muhammad as the last in a long line of prophets, and this lesson aims to present that view accurately while following the sequence of events that historians can trace.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: According to tradition, the Prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE into the clan of Hashim of the Quraysh tribe. Orphaned young, he was raised first by his grandfather and then by his uncle Abu Talib, and he grew up to work in the caravan trade, earning a reputation for honesty. He married Khadija, a respected merchant, who became his first supporter. Around the year 610 CE, while reflecting in a cave near Mecca, he reported receiving the first of many revelations through the angel Gabriel, calling him to proclaim the oneness of God, whom Arabic speakers call Allah. He began to preach a message of strict monotheism, moral responsibility, care for the poor, and a coming day of judgment. This message challenged the polytheism and the social order of Mecca, and many of the Quraysh leaders, whose standing rested partly on the shrine of many idols, grew hostile. Facing mounting pressure, in 622 CE the Prophet Muhammad and his followers migrated to the city of Yathrib, soon called Medina, an event known as the Hijra that marks year one of the Islamic calendar. There he built a community that united believers across tribal lines, and by his death in 632 CE much of Arabia had accepted Islam.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: A few dated milestones organize this life. Around 570 CE: birth in Mecca. Around 610 CE: the first revelation near Mecca, traditionally received through the angel Gabriel. The years that followed in Mecca were difficult, marked by ridicule and persecution of the early Muslims, some of whom briefly sought refuge in Christian Abyssinia (modern Ethiopia). 622 CE: the Hijra, the migration to Medina, the pivotal turning point and the start of the Hijri calendar. In Medina the Prophet Muhammad acted as both a religious and a community leader, and an agreement often called the Constitution of Medina set out relations among its groups. A series of conflicts with Mecca followed, ending in 630 CE when the Prophet Muhammad entered Mecca largely peacefully and the Kaaba was cleared of idols and rededicated to the worship of one God. 632 CE: his death in Medina, after a farewell pilgrimage. Key figures include Khadija, his first wife and earliest believer; his close companions Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali, who would later lead the community; and his cousin and son-in-law Ali in particular, whose standing matters for later history. These names and dates recur throughout the rest of the course.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In roughly what year was the Prophet Muhammad born, and in which city? 2) Who was his first wife and earliest supporter? 3) Around what year did the first revelation take place, and through whom is it traditionally said to have come? 4) What is the Hijra, and in what year did it occur? 5) Why did many Quraysh leaders oppose his message? 6) In what year did he die? Answers: 1) Around 570 CE, in Mecca. 2) Khadija, a respected merchant. 3) Around 610 CE, traditionally through the angel Gabriel. 4) The migration of the Prophet Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina, in 622 CE, which begins the Islamic calendar. 5) His call to worship one God challenged their polytheism and the social and economic order built around the many idols at the Kaaba. 6) In 632 CE, in Medina. Review any you missed, since the caliphates in later lessons begin exactly where this timeline ends, with the question of who should lead the community after the Prophet Muhammad.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the Hijra of 622 CE with the Prophet Muhammad's birth or with his later return to Mecca; the Hijra is specifically the migration to Medina. Mistake: assuming Islam spread only by force from the start; in Mecca the early Muslims were a persecuted minority, and the community first grew through preaching and migration. Mistake: describing Allah as a separate god; the word simply means God in Arabic, the same one creator worshipped in Jewish and Christian tradition. Exit ticket: (a) What event marks year one of the Islamic calendar, and what does it involve? (b) Name two close companions of the Prophet Muhammad who later led the community. Answers: (a) The Hijra, the migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. (b) Any two of Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali. Hold on to these companions' names; the next block of lessons follows them directly as the first caliphs and traces how a single Arabian community grew into a vast empire.

lessons.title: Core beliefs and practices: the Five Pillars and the Quran
lessons.grammar_note: Arabic religious terms are given in a simple spelling; the five daily prayers and the single holy book, the Quran, are described respectfully and accurately. Dates are CE.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the central beliefs of Islam and the five core practices that shape a Muslim's religious life, and describe the Quran and its place in the faith. By the end you will be able to state the meaning of tawhid, the oneness of God; list and briefly define the Five Pillars; and explain what the Quran is, how Muslims regard it, and how it is organized. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, recall how many Pillars there are and name any one you already know. As you read, aim for accuracy and respect: these are the living commitments of nearly two billion people today, and describing them clearly is the goal. You will finish able to distinguish belief, such as faith in one God and the prophets, from practice, such as prayer and fasting, and to see how the two fit together in daily life. This lesson also prepares you for later chapters, where religious practice travels with the expanding community across three continents.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: At the heart of Islam is tawhid, the belief in one God, Allah, who is the creator of all things and has no partner. Muslims believe God sent guidance through many prophets, from Adam, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus to the final prophet, the Prophet Muhammad, and that angels, revealed scriptures, and a Day of Judgment are part of the created order. The practical heart of the faith is the Five Pillars. The first is the Shahada, the sincere declaration that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the messenger of God. The second is Salat, formal prayer performed five times a day facing Mecca. The third is Zakat, the giving of a fixed share of one's wealth to those in need. The fourth is Sawm, fasting from dawn to sunset during the month of Ramadan. The fifth is Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca that every able Muslim who can afford it should make once in a lifetime. The Quran is the holy book of Islam, which Muslims believe to be the literal word of God revealed in Arabic to the Prophet Muhammad over about twenty-three years. It is organized into 114 chapters, called surahs, and is recited, memorized, and studied as the primary source of guidance, alongside the recorded sayings and example of the Prophet Muhammad, known as the hadith and the sunna.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Several ideas and terms deserve a closer look. The Shahada is both the entry into Islam and its daily affirmation; to say it sincerely is to become a Muslim. Salat structures the day with prayers at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, and night, and on Fridays the midday prayer is often performed together in a mosque. Zakat, usually calculated as a small percentage of accumulated wealth, is treated as a duty and a form of social justice rather than optional charity; voluntary giving beyond it is called sadaqa. Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, commemorates the beginning of the revelation of the Quran; the fast is broken each evening, and the month ends with the festival of Eid al-Fitr. The Hajj follows rites associated with Abraham and centers on the Kaaba in Mecca; the season is also marked by the festival of Eid al-Adha. The Quran itself was gathered into a single authoritative written text within a generation of the Prophet Muhammad's death. Together these beliefs and practices form a framework that is portable across cultures, which helps explain how Islam kept a shared core even as it spread among very different peoples in the centuries that followed.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does tawhid mean? 2) List the Five Pillars in order. 3) Which pillar is the declaration of faith? 4) During which month do Muslims fast from dawn to sunset? 5) What is the Quran, and into how many chapters is it divided? 6) What are the recorded sayings and example of the Prophet Muhammad called? Answers: 1) The oneness of God, the belief in one creator with no partner. 2) Shahada (declaration of faith), Salat (prayer), Zakat (almsgiving), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca). 3) The Shahada. 4) Ramadan. 5) The Quran is the holy book of Islam, believed by Muslims to be the word of God revealed to the Prophet Muhammad; it is divided into 114 chapters called surahs. 6) The hadith (sayings) and the sunna (example and practice). If you can recite the pillars in order and define tawhid, you have the core vocabulary that the rest of this course will build on when it describes religious life across the empires.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the pillars with beliefs; the Five Pillars are practices, while belief in one God, the prophets, and the Day of Judgment are matters of faith. Mistake: treating Zakat as optional charity; it is an obligatory share of wealth, distinct from voluntary giving. Mistake: assuming the Quran and the hadith are the same; the Quran is the revealed scripture, while the hadith records the Prophet Muhammad's own sayings and actions. Exit ticket: (a) Name the pillar that involves pilgrimage and the city it centers on. (b) In what language was the Quran revealed, and roughly over how long? Answers: (a) The Hajj, centered on Mecca and the Kaaba. (b) In Arabic, over about twenty-three years. With the beliefs and the Five Pillars in hand, you are ready for the first checkpoint, after which the course turns from faith to history and follows the community's leaders as Islam expands rapidly beyond Arabia.

questions.prompt: The cube-shaped shrine at the center of Mecca is the…
questions.explanation: The Kaaba is the shrine in Mecca toward which Muslims pray and which the Hajj centers on.

questions.prompt: According to tradition, the Prophet Muhammad received his first revelation through the angel…
questions.explanation: The angel Gabriel (Jibril) is traditionally said to have brought the first revelation around 610 CE.

questions.prompt: The Islamic declaration of faith is called the…
questions.explanation: The Shahada declares that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the messenger of God.

questions.prompt: Fasting from dawn to sunset during the month of Ramadan is which pillar?
questions.explanation: Sawm is the fourth pillar, the fast of Ramadan.

questions.prompt: The Quran is organized into chapters called…
questions.explanation: The Quran has 114 chapters known as surahs.

questions.prompt: The Hijra of 622 CE marks the start of…
questions.explanation: The migration from Mecca to Medina begins year one of the Hijri calendar.

lessons.title: The caliphates: Rashidun, Umayyad, and Abbasid
lessons.grammar_note: Caliph means successor or deputy; the realm a caliph rules is a caliphate. All dates are CE.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Follow Islamic history from the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE through three great caliphates: the Rashidun, the Umayyad, and the Abbasid. By the end you will be able to name the four Rashidun caliphs and describe the astonishingly rapid early expansion, explain how the Umayyads built the first hereditary dynasty from Damascus, and describe how the Abbasids shifted the center of the Islamic world to Baghdad. You will also understand the origin of the lasting distinction between Sunni and Shia Muslims, which traces back to disputes over who should lead the community. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, recall which city the Abbasids chose as their capital. As you read, keep the timeline in view: a single Arabian community in 632 CE became, within roughly a century, the ruler of an empire stretching from Spain to Central Asia. This lesson explains how that happened and who led it, setting up the Golden Age that follows.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: When the Prophet Muhammad died in 632 CE, the community had to decide who would lead it. The first four leaders, chosen from among his close companions, are called the Rashidun, or rightly guided, caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali. Under them, especially Umar, Muslim armies expanded with remarkable speed, taking the Levant and Egypt from the exhausted Byzantine Empire and conquering the entire Sasanian Persian Empire. A standardized written text of the Quran was established under Uthman. This era also saw internal conflict, including civil wars known as the fitna, and disputes over leadership that hardened into a lasting divide: Sunni Muslims accepted the line of caliphs as it developed, while Shia Muslims held that leadership belonged to Ali and his descendants. In 661 CE the Umayyad family took power and moved the capital to Damascus, creating the first hereditary dynasty and pushing the frontier west into North Africa and Spain and east toward the Indus and Central Asia. In 750 CE the Abbasid revolution overthrew the Umayyads and moved the capital to a new city, Baghdad. The Abbasids presided over a cosmopolitan, trade-rich empire and sponsored the learning that would define the Golden Age, ruling in various forms until the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258 CE.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Key dates and people anchor the three caliphates. 632 to 661 CE: the Rashidun caliphs, Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali, under whom Arab Muslim forces absorbed Persia and much of Byzantine territory. Umar is remembered for administrative reforms and the founding of garrison towns; Uthman for the authoritative compilation of the Quran; Ali for a contested reign that ended in civil war. 661 CE: Muawiya founds the Umayyad dynasty with its capital at Damascus. 711 CE: Umayyad forces cross into the Iberian Peninsula, beginning Islamic rule in Spain. The Umayyads also built one of Islam's earliest great monuments, the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed around 691 CE. 750 CE: the Abbasid revolution overturns the Umayyads; a surviving Umayyad prince escapes to Spain and founds a separate emirate there. 762 CE: the Abbasids found Baghdad, which becomes one of the world's largest and richest cities. 1258 CE: the Mongols capture and sack Baghdad, ending the Abbasid caliphate's real power. Across these centuries the Sunni and Shia distinction, rooted in the succession disputes of the first decades, became a permanent feature of the Islamic world that endures today.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does Rashidun mean, and who were the four Rashidun caliphs? 2) From which capital did the Umayyads rule? 3) In what year did Muslim forces first enter the Iberian Peninsula? 4) Which city did the Abbasids found as their capital, and in what year? 5) What event ended Abbasid power in 1258 CE? 6) What dispute lies at the root of the Sunni and Shia distinction? Answers: 1) Rightly guided; Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali. 2) Damascus. 3) 711 CE. 4) Baghdad, in 762 CE. 5) The Mongol capture and sack of Baghdad. 6) A disagreement over who should lead the community after the Prophet Muhammad: Sunnis accepted the developing line of caliphs, while Shia held that leadership belonged to Ali and his descendants. If you can place Damascus, Baghdad, and the year 711 CE on your mental map, you are ready for the Golden Age, which flowered above all in Abbasid Baghdad.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the caliphate was always hereditary; the first four Rashidun caliphs were chosen from among the Prophet Muhammad's companions, and hereditary rule began with the Umayyads. Mistake: treating the Sunni and Shia distinction as a late development; it grows directly out of the earliest succession disputes. Mistake: assuming the Abbasids destroyed the Umayyads everywhere; a branch survived in Spain and ruled there independently. Exit ticket: (a) Which dynasty ruled from Damascus, and which from Baghdad? (b) What happened to Baghdad in 1258 CE? Answers: (a) The Umayyads ruled from Damascus; the Abbasids ruled from Baghdad. (b) It was captured and sacked by the Mongols, ending the Abbasid caliphate's effective power. With the political framework of the caliphates in place, the next lesson steps inside Abbasid Baghdad to explore the scientific, mathematical, and philosophical achievements of the Islamic Golden Age.

lessons.title: The Islamic Golden Age
lessons.grammar_note: Scholars' names appear in a simple Arabic spelling with the familiar Latinized form in parentheses; all dates are CE.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the Islamic Golden Age, roughly the eighth through the thirteenth centuries CE, when scholars across the Muslim world advanced mathematics, science, medicine, and philosophy. By the end you will be able to explain the role of the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, connect al-Khwarizmi to the birth of algebra, identify Ibn Sina and his influence on medicine, and describe how the translation movement preserved and extended Greek, Persian, and Indian learning. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, recall which scholar is tied to the founding of algebra. As you read, notice that this was a collaborative, multicultural effort in which Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars worked side by side, and that many ideas we use today, from the word algebra to parts of our number system, passed through this period. The goal is to appreciate both the specific achievements and the conditions, wealth, stability, paper, and patronage, that made them possible, setting up the art and architecture explored in the next lesson.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: From the eighth century CE onward, the Abbasid capital of Baghdad became a magnet for scholars. A great library and research center often called the House of Wisdom, or Bayt al-Hikma, supported a vast translation movement that rendered Greek, Persian, Indian, and other works into Arabic, saving much ancient knowledge that might otherwise have been lost and building on it. In mathematics, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, working in ninth-century Baghdad, wrote a foundational treatise that gives us the word algebra, from the Arabic al-jabr, and his name, in Latinized form, gives us the word algorithm. Scholars also adopted and spread the decimal place-value number system, including the use of zero, drawn from Indian mathematics. In medicine, Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, compiled the Canon of Medicine, an encyclopedia that remained a standard reference for centuries, while al-Razi (Rhazes) made careful clinical observations. In optics, Ibn al-Haytham advanced the understanding of light and vision and stressed experiment. Astronomers refined star catalogs and instruments, and al-Biruni measured the Earth with striking accuracy. In philosophy, thinkers such as al-Farabi and Ibn Rushd (Averroes) engaged deeply with Aristotle, influencing later European thought. The spread of papermaking, learned from China, made books cheaper and learning more widely available across this connected world.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: A roster of figures defines the age. Al-Khwarizmi (around 780 to 850 CE): his book on al-jabr founded algebra as a discipline, and his treatise on Indian numerals helped spread the decimal system; the word algorithm descends from his name. Ibn Sina, or Avicenna (around 980 to 1037 CE): a Persian polymath whose Canon of Medicine organized medical knowledge so thoroughly that it was taught in Europe for centuries, and who also wrote major works of philosophy. Al-Razi, or Rhazes (around 854 to 925 CE): a physician known for clinical descriptions, including of smallpox and measles. Ibn al-Haytham, or Alhazen (around 965 to 1040 CE): a pioneer of optics and of experimental method. Al-Biruni (around 973 to 1050 CE): a scholar of astronomy, geography, and many sciences. Ibn Rushd, or Averroes (1126 to 1198 CE), working in Spain: a philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle shaped later European universities. The House of Wisdom in Baghdad symbolizes the institutional support behind this flowering, though learning also thrived in Cordoba, Cairo, Bukhara, and beyond. Papermaking, trade wealth, a shared Arabic scholarly language, and generous patronage combined to make the period one of the most creative in world history, with effects that reached far beyond the Muslim world.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What was the House of Wisdom, and in which city did it stand? 2) Which scholar is credited with founding algebra, and what word comes from his name? 3) Who wrote the Canon of Medicine, and by what name was he known in Europe? 4) From which culture did Muslim mathematicians adopt the decimal place-value system and the use of zero? 5) Which philosopher working in Spain wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle? 6) What technology, learned from China, helped spread books and learning? Answers: 1) A major library and translation and research center in Baghdad. 2) Al-Khwarizmi; the word algorithm comes from his name, and algebra from the title of his book. 3) Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna. 4) Indian mathematics. 5) Ibn Rushd, known as Averroes. 6) Papermaking. If you can link al-Khwarizmi to algebra and Ibn Sina to medicine, you have grasped two of the age's signature contributions and are ready to see how the same culture expressed itself in art and architecture.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: imagining this learning was the work of one group alone; Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars collaborated, and the knowledge drew on Greek, Persian, and Indian sources. Mistake: thinking the translation movement merely copied older works; scholars corrected, extended, and created new fields such as algebra. Mistake: assuming all this happened only in Baghdad; Cordoba, Cairo, and Central Asian cities were also major centers. Exit ticket: (a) Give the two English words that descend from al-Khwarizmi and the title of his book. (b) Name the medical encyclopedia that was taught in Europe for centuries and its author. Answers: (a) Algorithm (from his name) and algebra (from al-jabr in his book's title). (b) The Canon of Medicine, by Ibn Sina (Avicenna). Carry forward the sense of a confident, connected civilization; the next lesson shows how that confidence took visible form in mosques, palaces, calligraphy, and the brilliant culture of Al-Andalus in Spain.

lessons.title: Islamic art, architecture, literature, and Al-Andalus
lessons.grammar_note: Building terms such as mihrab, minbar, and minaret are introduced in context; Al-Andalus is the historical Arabic name for Muslim Iberia. Dates are CE.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognize the main features of Islamic art and architecture and describe the rich culture of Al-Andalus, or Islamic Spain. By the end you will be able to explain why calligraphy, geometric pattern, and arabesque became central art forms, identify the key parts of a mosque, and name landmark buildings such as the Great Mosque of Cordoba and the Alhambra. You will also be able to tell the broad story of Al-Andalus from 711 to 1492 CE and describe the period of relatively shared life among Muslims, Jews, and Christians sometimes called convivencia. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, recall the Arabic name for Islamic Spain. As you read, aim to see art and architecture not as decoration alone but as expressions of belief, especially the preference in religious settings for pattern and the written word over images of living beings. This lesson links the Golden Age of ideas to the culture that made those ideas beautiful and visible, and it carries the story to the western edge of the Muslim world.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Islamic art developed a distinctive visual language shaped partly by a religious preference, in sacred settings, for avoiding images of people and animals, which turned artistic energy toward calligraphy, geometry, and stylized plant forms. Arabic calligraphy became the highest art, since it carried the words of the Quran; intricate geometric patterns and flowing vegetal designs called arabesque covered walls, books, ceramics, and textiles. In architecture, the mosque is the central building, typically featuring a prayer hall oriented toward Mecca, a niche called the mihrab marking that direction, a pulpit called the minbar, a courtyard, and often one or more towers called minarets from which the call to prayer is given. Domes, horseshoe and pointed arches, and honeycomb-like muqarnas vaulting are recurring features. Al-Andalus, the Arabic name for the parts of the Iberian Peninsula under Muslim rule from 711 CE, became one of the most sophisticated societies in medieval Europe. Its capital, Cordoba, grew into a great center of learning, with libraries, paved streets, and the magnificent Great Mosque. For long stretches, Muslims, Jews, and Christians lived and worked together in a comparatively tolerant society, a period often called convivencia, which produced thinkers such as Averroes and the Jewish philosopher Maimonides. Christian kingdoms gradually expanded southward in the long process called the Reconquista, and the last Muslim state, Granada, fell in 1492 CE.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Landmark works and moments bring this culture to life. The Great Mosque of Cordoba, begun in the eighth century CE, is famous for its forest of red and white double arches and shows the confidence of Umayyad Spain. The Alhambra in Granada, built mainly by the Nasrid dynasty in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries CE, is a palace and fortress celebrated for its courtyards, water features, and delicate stucco and tile work. The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (around 691 CE) is among the earliest masterpieces of Islamic architecture. In literature, the collection of stories known as One Thousand and One Nights gathered tales from across the Muslim world, while poets such as the Persian Omar Khayyam and later the mystic Rumi became world famous. Al-Andalus produced the philosopher Ibn Rushd (Averroes) and was home to the Jewish scholar Maimonides, both born in Cordoba. The year 1492 CE marks the fall of Granada, the end of nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule in Spain. Across all these works runs a shared aesthetic: the beauty of the written word, the harmony of geometry, and a love of light, water, and garden that expressed a vision of paradise. This heritage still shapes architecture and design today.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why did calligraphy and geometric pattern become central to Islamic art? 2) Name three parts of a typical mosque. 3) What is the Arabic name for Islamic Spain, and when did Muslim rule there begin and end? 4) Which famous palace stands in Granada, and which dynasty built most of it? 5) What is convivencia? 6) Name one philosopher and one collection of stories associated with the medieval Muslim world. Answers: 1) In sacred settings there was a preference to avoid images of living beings, so artists focused on the beauty of the written word, geometry, and arabesque. 2) Any three of: the mihrab (niche toward Mecca), the minbar (pulpit), a courtyard, the prayer hall, and a minaret. 3) Al-Andalus; Muslim rule began in 711 CE and ended with the fall of Granada in 1492 CE. 4) The Alhambra, built mainly by the Nasrid dynasty. 5) A period of comparatively shared and tolerant life among Muslims, Jews, and Christians in Al-Andalus. 6) For example, Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and the collection One Thousand and One Nights.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing Islam forbids all images; the preference to avoid depicting living beings applies mainly to religious art, and figurative painting did appear in some secular settings. Mistake: romanticizing convivencia as perfect harmony; it was a real but uneven coexistence that included periods of tension and conflict. Mistake: confusing the Great Mosque of Cordoba with the Alhambra; the first is a mosque in Cordoba, the second a palace in Granada. Exit ticket: (a) What does the mihrab in a mosque indicate? (b) What happened in 1492 CE in Al-Andalus? Answers: (a) The direction of Mecca, which worshippers face in prayer. (b) Granada, the last Muslim state in Spain, fell to the Christian kingdoms, ending nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule. With the western and cultural reach of the Muslim world in view, the final lesson moves east and forward in time to the great early-modern empires and the diverse Islamic world of today.

lessons.title: Empires and the modern Islamic world: Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal
lessons.grammar_note: The Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal empires are sometimes grouped as the gunpowder empires; place names such as Istanbul and Isfahan are given in their common English forms. Dates are CE.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the three great early-modern Muslim empires, the Ottoman, the Safavid, and the Mughal, and trace how the Islamic world moved from their height into the modern era. By the end you will be able to place each empire on the map and name a signature ruler or monument, explain the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 CE and the empire's long reach, note the Safavid adoption of Shia Islam as a state religion in Persia, and connect the Mughals to the Taj Mahal in India. You will also be able to outline, in broad strokes, the later decline of these empires, the impact of European colonialism, the end of the caliphate in 1924 CE, and the diversity of the roughly two billion Muslims in the world today. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, recall the year Constantinople fell and the monument linked to Shah Jahan. This closing lesson ties the long history together and brings it up to the present with accuracy and respect.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: By the sixteenth century CE, three powerful Muslim empires dominated a broad band of the world, and historians sometimes call them the gunpowder empires for their use of artillery. The Ottoman Empire, founded around 1299 CE in Anatolia, captured Constantinople in 1453 CE, renamed it as its capital, and grew to span southeastern Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa; under Suleiman the Magnificent in the sixteenth century it reached its height. The Safavid Empire, founded in 1501 CE by Shah Ismail in Persia, made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, shaping the religious map of the region to this day, and made Isfahan a jewel of a capital. The Mughal Empire, founded in 1526 CE by Babur in the Indian subcontinent, ruled a vast, wealthy, and largely non-Muslim population; the emperor Akbar is remembered for tolerance and administration, and Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife. From the eighteenth century these empires weakened under internal strain and growing European power. European colonial rule spread across much of the Muslim world, the Ottoman Empire fell after the First World War, and in 1924 CE the Turkish republic abolished the caliphate. In the twentieth century new nation-states emerged, and oil transformed several economies. Today Islam is a global faith of nearly two billion people, diverse in culture, language, and practice.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Several dates and figures organize the early-modern and modern story. 1453 CE: the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captures Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire; the great church of Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque, and the city, later called Istanbul, becomes the Ottoman capital. The sixteenth century: Suleiman the Magnificent presides over Ottoman law, culture, and expansion. 1501 CE: Shah Ismail founds the Safavid Empire and establishes Twelver Shia Islam in Persia; Isfahan flourishes as a capital of art and architecture. 1526 CE: Babur founds the Mughal Empire; his grandson Akbar (reigned 1556 to 1605 CE) builds a tolerant, well-run state, and Shah Jahan (reigned 1628 to 1658 CE) builds the Taj Mahal around 1632 to 1653 CE. The eighteenth and nineteenth centuries: all three empires decline as European powers advance, and much of the Muslim world comes under colonial rule. 1922 to 1924 CE: the Ottoman sultanate and then the caliphate are abolished as the Turkish republic is founded under Mustafa Kemal Ataturk. The twentieth and twenty-first centuries: independence movements, the rise of nation-states, the oil economy, and large Muslim populations in countries such as Indonesia, Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh, as well as sizable communities in Europe and the Americas, define a varied global community.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three early-modern Muslim empires and the regions each ruled. 2) In what year did the Ottomans capture Constantinople, and who led the conquest? 3) Which empire made Twelver Shia Islam its state religion, and in what year was it founded? 4) Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal, and for whom? 5) What happened to the caliphate in 1924 CE? 6) Roughly how many Muslims are there in the world today, and name two countries with large Muslim populations. Answers: 1) The Ottomans in Anatolia, the Middle East, southeastern Europe, and North Africa; the Safavids in Persia; the Mughals in the Indian subcontinent. 2) 1453 CE, led by Sultan Mehmed II. 3) The Safavid Empire, founded in 1501 CE. 4) Shah Jahan, as a tomb for his wife. 5) It was abolished by the new Turkish republic under Ataturk. 6) Nearly two billion; examples include Indonesia, Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh. If you can place these three empires and summarize the move into the modern era, you have completed the arc of the course.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming all Muslims are Arabs; the largest Muslim populations today are in South and Southeast Asia, and Arabs are a minority of the global community. Mistake: treating the Sunni and Shia distinction as modern; recall it began with the earliest succession disputes and was reinforced when the Safavids made Shia Islam a state religion. Mistake: thinking the empires fell suddenly; they declined gradually over generations amid internal strain and European pressure. Exit ticket: (a) Match each empire to a signature monument or capital: Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal. (b) What two broad forces reshaped the Muslim world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries? Answers: (a) Ottoman, Istanbul and Hagia Sophia; Safavid, Isfahan; Mughal, the Taj Mahal. (b) European colonialism and, later, the rise of independent nation-states, alongside the transforming effect of oil. This completes the journey from pre-Islamic Arabia to the present; take the final checkpoint to review the full span of Islamic history and civilization.

questions.prompt: The first four caliphs after the Prophet Muhammad are collectively known as the…
questions.explanation: The Rashidun, or rightly guided, caliphs were Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali.

questions.prompt: The Umayyad caliphate ruled from its capital at…
questions.explanation: The Umayyads governed from Damascus; the Abbasids later moved the capital to Baghdad.

questions.prompt: The House of Wisdom, a great center of translation and learning, stood in…
questions.explanation: The Bayt al-Hikma in Abbasid Baghdad anchored the translation movement of the Golden Age.

questions.prompt: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) is best known for an influential medical encyclopedia called the…
questions.explanation: The Canon of Medicine remained a standard reference in Europe for centuries.

questions.prompt: The last Muslim state in Spain, Granada, fell in…
questions.explanation: Granada fell in 1492 CE, ending nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule in Al-Andalus.

questions.prompt: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan is famous for building the…
questions.explanation: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in India as a tomb for his wife, around 1632 to 1653 CE.
